items.text:
The Invention of the Printing Press
Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand. A single book could take months to produce, so books were rare and expensive, and few people outside churches and universities could read. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press that used movable metal type. Individual letters could be arranged to form a page, inked and pressed onto paper, and then rearranged for the next page.
The effects were dramatic. Within fifty years, millions of books had been printed across Europe. As books became cheaper, more people learned to read, and new ideas in science and religion spread far faster than before. Some historians argue that the printing press made possible the scientific revolution of the following centuries, because scientists could share and check one another's results.
Gutenberg himself did not become rich. He borrowed heavily to build his workshop, and a dispute with his business partner cost him much of his equipment.

tr.zh:
印刷機的發明
十五世紀以前，歐洲的書是手抄的。一本書可能要花幾個月才能完成，所以書既稀少又昂貴，教會和大學以外的人很少識字。大約 1450 年，古騰堡發展出使用活字金屬字模的印刷機。一個個字母可以排成一頁，上墨後壓印到紙上，再重新排列印下一頁。
影響十分巨大。五十年內，歐洲各地印了數百萬本書。書變便宜後，更多人學會識字，科學和宗教的新思想傳播得比以前快得多。有些歷史學家認為，印刷機促成了之後幾個世紀的科學革命，因為科學家能分享並檢驗彼此的成果。
古騰堡本人並沒有致富。他為了建工坊借了大筆錢，和生意夥伴的糾紛又讓他失去許多設備。

options: To show a long-term effect of printing
To explain how Gutenberg built the press
questions.zh: 說明印刷機的長遠影響。

questions.q: What can be inferred about Gutenberg?

items.text:
How Cities Shape Bird Songs
Birds use songs to attract mates and defend territories, so it matters that other birds can hear them. In cities, however, songs must compete with traffic and construction noise, which is mostly low in pitch. Researchers studying great tits in several European cities found that urban birds sang at a higher pitch than birds of the same species in nearby forests.
One explanation is that higher notes are easier to hear above low-pitched noise. Some urban birds also sing louder, and others sing earlier in the morning, before traffic begins.
These changes may have costs. Female birds of some species prefer low-pitched songs, which may signal a larger, healthier male. A city male that sings higher may therefore be heard more easily but chosen less often. Scientists are still studying whether such changes are learned by young birds or are becoming part of their genes.

tr.zh:
城市如何改變鳥鳴
鳥用歌聲吸引配偶、保衛地盤，所以讓其他鳥聽得到很重要。但在城市裡，歌聲必須和交通、施工噪音競爭，而這些噪音大多是低音。研究人員觀察歐洲幾個城市的大山雀，發現城市裡的鳥比附近森林的同種鳥唱得更高。
一種解釋是高音比較容易在低沉的噪音中被聽見。有些城市鳥也唱得更大聲，有些則在交通開始前、更早的清晨唱歌。
這些改變可能有代價。有些鳥種的雌鳥偏好低音歌聲，因為那可能代表雄鳥較大、較健康。因此，唱得較高的城市雄鳥也許比較容易被聽到，卻比較少被選上。科學家仍在研究這些改變是幼鳥學來的，還是正成為基因的一部分。

items.text:
The Domestication of Wheat
About 10,000 years ago, people in the region known as the Fertile Crescent, in what is now the Middle East, began to grow wheat instead of only gathering it from the wild. This change was one of the most important steps in human history, because farming allowed people to stay in one place and build permanent villages.
Wild wheat has a problem for farmers: when its seeds are ripe, the head of the plant breaks apart and the seeds fall to the ground. This helps the plant spread, but it makes harvesting difficult. Occasionally, however, a plant had a mutation that kept its seeds attached. When early farmers harvested, they naturally collected more seeds from these plants and planted them the next year.
Over many generations, this unintentional selection produced wheat that kept its seeds until it was cut. Archaeologists can recognize domesticated wheat because the remains of its seed heads show a rough break, made by people threshing the grain, rather than the smooth break of wild wheat.

tr.zh:
小麥的馴化
大約一萬年前，在今日中東一帶稱為「肥沃月彎」的地區，人們開始種植小麥，而不只是從野外採集。這個改變是人類史上最重要的一步之一，因為農耕讓人們能定居一地，建立永久的村落。
野生小麥對農夫來說有個問題：種子成熟時，麥穗會散開，種子掉到地上。這有助於植物散播，卻讓收割很困難。不過偶爾會有植株發生突變，讓種子留在穗上。早期農夫收割時，自然會從這些植株收集到較多種子，隔年再種下。
經過許多世代，這種無意的選擇產生了收割前種子不會掉落的小麥。考古學家能辨認出馴化的小麥，因為其麥穗殘骸是人們脫粒造成的粗糙斷面，而不是野生小麥的平滑斷面。

items.text:
The Silk Road
The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of trade routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe for more than 1,500 years. It takes its name from Chinese silk, which was highly valued in Rome, but many other goods traveled along it, including spices, glass, paper and horses.
Few merchants traveled the entire distance. Instead, goods usually passed through many hands, each trader carrying them part of the way before selling them to the next. As a result, prices rose steadily as goods moved west, and a piece of silk could be worth many times its original price by the time it reached the Mediterranean.
Perhaps even more important than the goods were the ideas that spread along the routes. Religions such as Buddhism traveled from India into China, and technologies such as papermaking moved westward. Historians therefore describe the Silk Road as one of the first examples of globalization.

tr.zh:
絲路
絲路不是一條路，而是一個貿易路線網絡，連接中國與中亞、中東和歐洲長達一千五百多年。它因中國絲綢而得名，絲綢在羅馬極受珍視，但沿路運送的還有許多其他貨物，包括香料、玻璃、紙和馬匹。
很少有商人走完全程。貨物通常經過許多人之手，每個商人只運一段路，再賣給下一個人。因此貨物往西走，價格就不斷上漲，一塊絲綢到達地中海時，可能值原價的好幾倍。
比貨物更重要的，或許是沿路傳播的思想。佛教等宗教從印度傳入中國，造紙等技術則往西傳。因此歷史學家把絲路形容為最早的全球化例子之一。

questions.q: The word "steadily" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to

It connected distant regions through trade and ideas.
questions.zh: 連接遠方地區、交流貨物與思想。
